newsitem.title: USA: Exide may seek "white knight" to deter Danaher bid.
newsitem.headline: Exide may seek "white knight" to deter Danaher bid.

text.p: Danaher Corp's unsolicited takeover bid for Exide Electronics Group Inc is a proven, successful strategy for Danaher, but may force Exide into the arms of a friendly buyer, analysts said.
Danaher announced today that its $20 and $22 per share tender offers for Exide had been privately rejected.

The play is known on Wall Street as a "bear hug" and is designed to foment stockholder agitation. Once a tender offer becomes public knowledge, shareholders may decide they want better value for their stock and pressure the company to accept an offer from one suitor or another.

"Danaher is an extraordinarily well-run business. It has a long history of doing 'bear hug' deals and they are thorough. Since 1990, they have made about 25 acquisitions and all have been accretive in the first year," noted NatWest analyst Cliff Ransom.

DQE Inc, a Pittsburgh-based electric utility, owns about 10 percent of Exide's outstanding shares through a subsidiary, making it a leading candidate to become a "white knight" Exide buyer, analysts said.
Danaher said it owns about 397,000 of Exide's approximately 10.1 million shares outstanding.
Duquense Enterprises, the strategic investment unit of DQE, owns 1.1 million Exide shares, or 10 percent.
A DQE spokeswoman had no immediate comment.
Also cited as a potential friendly buyer was American Power Conversion Corp, which shares with Exide some uninterruptable-power gear markets, particularly those related to computers.
An APC spokeswoman was not immediately available to comment.
Interstate Johnson/Lane analyst Dimitri Triantafyllides said Exide is defending its independence from a position of financial weakness.
"Exide has had a lot of growth through acquisitions and has assumed a lot of leverage in doing so. That has hurt their bottom line and near-term performance," he said.
The offer at $20 per share "implies equity value of $220 million and there is another $220 million in long-term debt for a total enterprise value of $440 million," he said.
In late May, Standard & Poor's said revised its Exide outlook to negative because of weaker than expected financial performance.

NatWest's Ransom noted that over 40 percent of Danaher, a Washington, D.C.-based maker of tools, components and process/environmental controls, is owned by management and the board and is "one of exactly three companies where every member of the board owns more than $1 million in stock."

"Exide (stock) has been over 25 three times since 1992, and it was at 12 and a fraction before this announcement. It leads me to believe the credibility of Exide is not high. Exide, whether they like it or not, is in play."
Exide shares rocketed 7-3/4 to 20-5/8 in late afternoon Nasdaq trade, while Danaher edged up 1/16 to 49-7/8 on the New York Stock Exchange.
